name: Erik Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Erik, 27. I'm a second-year apprentice lineworker, but I don't work for the electricity company directly. I'm with a contractor that builds new lines for them, and we get sent out on storm jobs too. I live with my girlfriend Sara, who's a dental hygienist.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Then let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the contract. This autumn we're building a new line out to a solar farm, so it's a 5 a.m. start, an hour's drive, then setting poles, framing crossarms and stringing wire all day. My foreman Luis runs a tight crew and I'm the one hauling and rigging on the ground. My girlfriend Sara cleans teeth and I fix wires. We joke that we've both got jobs a computer can't do, but I've stopped laughing as hard.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly because of the contract side. When a big job ends, the contractor lays people off till the next one. Last January I was home five weeks with no pay, and we lived off savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So basically today, just carrying on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what most of the crew expected, a lot of fuss for a better search engine. I'd say it at the yard and maybe make a joke online. Not a big deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI was never my problem. My problem is a contractor who sends me home for five weeks every January without pay. That stays exactly the same in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the next apprentice opening on the electricity company's own crews, because in-house crews don't get laid off between jobs. I'd keep topping savings back up after last winter, about 250 a month. And I'd keep doing the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but about the usual stuff. Not about AI at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said savings carried you last winter. How much is there now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three months of our half of the bills. Sara earns a bit more than me, so we'd get through another January, but I hate dipping into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the routine automation in this picture touch for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our timesheets and the safety forms, probably. Luis spends Friday afternoons typing them up. I use a chatbot now and then to tidy up a CV or plan a drive, so I'd use it for that too.

say: AI turned out to be **a lot of fuss** for a better search engine.
I'd make a joke about it at the **yard** and move on.
think: AI was never my problem; **unpaid winters** between contracts are the real worry.
The contractor's **layoffs** between jobs stay exactly the same.
do: Apply for the next **in-house apprentice** opening at the electricity company.
Rebuild savings with about **250 a month** after last winter's layoff.
feel: **Uneasy** about contract layoffs, not about AI.
S0.quote: AI was never my problem. My problem is a contractor who sends me home for five weeks every January without pay.
fieldNote: His insecurity comes from **contract work**, which AI Plateau does nothing to fix.
The real goal is moving **in-house** to the electricity company's own crews.
He is a **light AI user**, mainly for CVs and route planning.

steps.text: Apply for the next in-house apprentice opening at the electricity company
Rebuild savings with 250 a month after the January layoff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one's more mixed for a contractor, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for line crews, because everything needs more power, and someone has to build the lines. I'd say the office jobs will feel it, not us. I'd say that fairly confidently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more building work, honestly. Solar farms, battery sites, data centres all need new lines. But the contractor would use AI to plan crews tighter, so fewer quiet weeks paid and more hire-and-fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying in-house, every opening. I'd learn whatever AI planning app the contractor brings in, once Luis says it's worth the bother. And I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not bad, just watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the contractor side would feel it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our estimator Phil prices every job by hand. If a computer does that in a minute, my boss wins more bids, and I get more work. Phil's the one who'd be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You think it could mean more work. Does that make you calmer about the layoffs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. More bids means fewer gaps. But tighter planning means they'd only keep exactly the crew they need, and I'm the junior.

say: New **power lines** for solar and data centres mean more work for crews.
**Office jobs** will feel it before line crews do.
think: AI pricing could win **more bids** and fill the gaps between jobs.
Tighter planning means less slack for a **junior** like me.
do: Keep applying for **every in-house** opening at the electricity company.
Learn the contractor's **planning app** once Luis says it's worth it.
feel: **Uneasy** and watchful, but not worried for his own trade.
S1.quote: Our estimator Phil prices every job by hand. If a computer does that in a minute, my boss wins more bids, and I get more work.
fieldNote: He sees **grid growth** as more work and office roles as the ones exposed.
Weighs more bids against **tighter crews** with honest balance.
Waits for his foreman's **approval** before learning new tools, typical of a steady adopter.

steps.text: Keep applying for every in-house opening at the electricity company
Learn the contractor's AI planning app once Luis approves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then robots three years later. That's 2031, when I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules so the crews that built the grid get first pick of the new jobs. I'd say it at the yard and maybe sign something online. I'd be less jokey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Contractors buy robots first, because that's how they win bids. I'd want to be inside the electricity company before 2031, not outside waiting by the phone. The thinking AI in 2028 would take Phil and the planners, and then it's us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to get in-house in the first year, even taking a pay cut. I'd stop eating out and skip the holiday we'd planned, which saves about 1,500. All of it goes into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but it'd depend on someone else saying yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think contract crews would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a contractor lives on price. The minute a robot crew is cheaper than us, they bid with the robots. The electricity company's own crews have union rules and are slower to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sara say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sara would say she's fine because nobody wants a robot in their mouth, and she's probably right for a while. Then she'd tell me to stop moping and send the application.

say: The crews who built the grid should get **first pick** of new jobs.
I'd say it at the yard and **sign petitions** online.
think: Contractors will buy **robots first** to win bids.
I need to be **in-house** before 2031, not waiting by the phone.
do: Move **in-house** within the first year, even with a pay cut.
Skip the planned holiday to save about **1,500**.
Stop eating out and **bank** every spare bit of pay.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan that depends on someone else saying yes.
S2.quote: Contractors buy robots first, because that's how they win bids. I'd want to be inside the electricity company before 2031, not outside waiting by the phone.
fieldNote: His sharpest insight is that **contract crews** are first exposed because they compete on price.
Sees in-house **union rules** as slowing robots, a pragmatic rather than political view.
Sara's **hands-on** job steadies the household, at least for a while.

steps.text: Move to an in-house electricity company crew, even for less pay
Skip the planned holiday to save about 1,500
Bank every spare bit of pay in the joint savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's enough to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so the industry should plan training with the crews now. I'd say that at work and leave the politics to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from climbing poles to fixing substations, because the more complicated the kit, the later the robot comes for it. Robots in 2034 means I've got about seven years to get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get in-house by 2027, then ask to start the substation technician course, which is about two years part-time and mostly paid by the company. I'd save 300 a month. I'd use AI tools a bit more for the theory, now that everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be too occupied to dwell on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why substations? What's different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every substation's a bit different, old relays, new relays, odd wiring from the 1970s. It's fiddly diagnostic work, part thinking and part hands-on. A robot that strings wire would come years before one that sorts out a 50-year-old switchyard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be giving up line work you clearly enjoy. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I like being up a pole on a sunny day. But I'd take a job I keep over a job I like.

I'd say that at work and leave **politics** to others.

do: Get **in-house** by 2027 and then start the substation technician course.
Save **300 a month** while studying part-time.

feel: **Anxious** but too busy to dwell on it.
S3.quote: I'd move from climbing poles to fixing substations, because the more complicated the kit, the later the robot comes for it.
fieldNote: Plans a move toward **diagnostic** work, which mixes thinking and hands-on.

Picks up AI more once **others** do, as expected for a steady adopter.

steps.text: Get onto an in-house crew by 2027
Start the two-year substation technician course part-time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a career's worth of planning, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out with ten years' notice. I'd tell the younger apprentices to plan. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to get qualified, get inside the company and get one level up. I'd do it in that order. I'd be 37 when the thinking AI lands and 40 when the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify by 2028 and keep working as a lineworker. Around 2031 I'd start the substation course. And I'd put 150 a month into a pension fund, which I don't do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it's far enough off that I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So you'd do the same moves as before, just slower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. With ten years I don't need to rush in-house or take a pay cut. I'd move when a good spot opened up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned money. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pension and an index fund, which is just a cheap fund that buys a bit of every big company. If robots make companies richer, I'd want a small piece of that.

say: With ten years' notice, **no one** in the trade should be caught out.
I'd tell the younger **apprentices** to plan their next step now.
think: Ten years is enough to **qualify**, move in-house and move up.
I'd be **40** when robots arrive, with time to have moved on.
do: Qualify by **2028** and keep working as a lineworker.
Put **150 a month** into a pension and index fund.
feel: **Uneasy** but sleeping fine, with the change far off.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to get qualified, get inside the company and get one level up. I'd do it in that order.
fieldNote: Same plan as the five-year picture but **without a pay cut** or rush.
Wants a **share** of robot profits through an index fund.
His **centre** outlook shows in practical advice, not political demands.

steps.text: Qualify by 2028 and keep working on line crews

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm a contractor, and contractors go first. What would help is a fair way for contract crews to get onto the electricity company's own crews, and training for substation work that the company pays for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about contract workers specifically. Everyone thinks lineworkers all work for the power company, but a lot of us don't, and we'd be the first to feel it.

headlineQuote: My girlfriend Sara cleans teeth and I fix wires. We joke that we've both got jobs a computer can't do, but I've stopped laughing as hard.
portrait: Erik is a 27-year-old **second-year apprentice** with a contractor that builds lines for the electricity company.
He lives with his girlfriend Sara, a **dental hygienist**, and dreads the contractor's winter **layoffs**.
His constant aim is moving **in-house**, where crews aren't laid off between jobs.
In faster AGI pictures he expects **contract crews** to get robots first.
His long-run plan is **substation work**, where complex old kit delays robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because contractors adopt robots first to win bids.
whatWouldHelp: A fair route for **contract crews** onto in-house crews.
